title: The Shape of Forgiveness
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 27 of 40
content:
The hill was steeper than I remembered.

Iroh had said we were going to see the view. He had packed tea, an offering bowl, and a folded cloth in the careful way he packed things when he didn't want to talk about them. I knew where we were going before we left the shop.

The wind was strong enough to pull loose strands of hair across my face. Near the top, Iroh stopped to let a small procession pass. A family carried flowers and a plain wooden box, speaking softly among themselves. They didn't recognize him, or perhaps they did and chose not to say anything.

"Should we wait?" I asked.

"Yes."

We sat on a flat stone just off the path. Below us, Ba Sing Se went about its business: carts crossing the roads, workers calling to one another, kitchens starting their afternoon fires. It felt wrong and right that the city could be so alive while he was carrying grief up a hill.

When the others had gone, we reached the memorial place. Iroh brushed the leaves away without hurrying. He set down the bowl and stood still.

I didn't reach for his hand. I wanted to, badly. My wish to comfort him was not more important than his right to choose how this moment went.

He began talking about Lu Ten's laugh.

Not the solemn version I had heard when other people spoke of his son. A ridiculous, helpless laugh. A laugh that once startled a messenger so much he dropped a stack of papers in front of the entire officers' tent.

"What made him laugh?" I asked.

"Me," Iroh said, and looked almost offended by the memory. "I was attempting to look important."

"That does sound funny."

"I was a very impressive general."

"Apparently not impressive enough."

He smiled. Then the smile broke apart.

"I cannot remember the exact sound anymore," he said.

The admission seemed to cost him more than the walk. I looked at the offering bowl because looking straight at him felt too much like expecting him to perform his grief.

"Do you want me to say something?" I asked.

"No. Not yet."

We watched the grass bend. I thought of the stories people told about forgiveness, how neatly they arranged the moment when pain was supposed to stop hurting. Nothing neat happened on the hill. Iroh was a man who had made terrible choices in a terrible war, who had loved his child, and who could not undo either of those facts.

He sat down beside the bowl.

"Some mornings I wonder whether a better father would have been a worse general," he said. "And whether being that father would have brought my son home."

I had no answer. It was hard not to offer one anyway.

"That sounds like something nobody can prove," I said at last.

"Yes."

"I don't want to tell you to forgive yourself because it would make this easier for me."

He closed his eyes briefly.

"Thank you."

A bird landed on a branch above us, shouted at nothing, and flew away. Iroh made a startled noise that was almost a laugh.

"Even the birds are impatient with my solemnity."

"I think it was offended by my tea."

"You brewed the tea?"

"You left me the kettle."

"A dangerous delegation."

Iroh held the cup between his hands. For a while I thought he had no more words.

"When Lu Ten was young," he said at last, "he wrote letters home from training. Most of them were astonishingly dull."

"Dull?"

"Descriptions of weather. Food. Someone forgetting his boots. I kept every one."

I looked at the memorial stone. "I don't think that sounds dull."

"Neither did I. I liked knowing he had lived another ordinary day."

"Were there any you didn't understand?" I asked.
"Many. He referred to people by nicknames I never learned. Once he told me a tent had been taken prisoner by the wind. I spent a full hour wondering which unit had lost its shelter."
"Did you ask?"
"I wrote an excellent, very stern inquiry."
"Of course you did."
"He sent back a drawing of a tent with chains on its wrists."
Iroh smiled at his cup. I could picture his younger self, surrounded by maps, taking the time to argue with a drawing. The image made my throat tighten in a way I could not explain.
"Sometimes," he said, "I fear that if I tell you the funny things, you will forget what the army did."
"I won't."
"Or that you will think I was always the person you know now."
"I won't do that either."
He turned the cup once, testing its warmth against his palms. The wind kept lifting the folded cloth at the edge of the offering bowl. I held it steady so he would not have to set the cup down.
"You can love him without telling me a clean story about yourself," I said.
"An inconvenient kindness," Iroh replied. "You have learned from some very troublesome company."
I waited until he offered a corner of the cloth. Then I sat beside him and helped keep it in place. The bowl, the letters, and his memories belonged to him; I could share the wind without claiming anything else.

The wind moved the flowers along the path. Below us a cart rattled through the street, its driver calling for someone to close a gate. Ba Sing Se was still full of people worrying about little things. Iroh watched the city with an expression I hadn't learned to name.

"His laugh was very loud," he said. "Louder than mine, if you can imagine that."

"Unlikely."

"An outrageous judgment."

"He was your son. I assume he inherited the worst parts of your humor."

Iroh laughed, and then his eyes filled with tears. He covered them with his hand. I watched the clouds rather than making him perform grief where I could see it.

"I'm glad you told me," I said.

"It doesn't make a very grand story."

"I don't need a grand one."

He spoke again about a little wooden fish Lu Ten had brought home from a market. It had been badly carved, with one side larger than the other. Iroh had put it on a shelf until the war scattered everything he owned. Remembering it hurt because it had been part of a life with no reason to expect an ending.

I wanted to say that memories couldn't be taken away, but that wasn't true either. People forgot things. Faces changed. Words disappeared. Sometimes a small object was simply gone.

"Would you like to draw it?" I asked.

He considered. "My drawing is terrible."

"So is mine."

We took out the notebook I carried and spent a few minutes arguing about the shape of a fish. Our drawings were awful. His had a tail that looked suspiciously like a teapot spout.

"Magnificent," I said.

"Clearly."

I left the page with him. He folded it carefully and put it in his sleeve. It wasn't a substitute for the toy or the boy who had loved it. It was something he'd chosen to make today.

When he offered his hand, I took it. He didn't ask me to solve his sorrow. I didn't ask him to make the hill into a monument to our romance. We stayed together until he was ready to walk down, and I let the rest of the afternoon be quiet.

We poured a little into the bowl and shared the rest. I told him about the first time I had tried to make a memorial into a task list, how I had wanted to be useful so badly that I nearly forgot why I was there. He listened without turning my confession into a lesson.

"I don't know where I belong in this part of your life," I admitted.

"Beside me, when you wish to be."

"Not as a replacement for anybody."

"Never."

I took a breath. "I've said before that I'm ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory. Loving more than one person doesn't make any of them interchangeable. I don't want to treat Lu Ten's memory that way either. Your grief has a place. So do I. Those aren't competing seats."

He looked at me for a long moment.

"You explain yourself in such complicated ways," he said.

"You're the one with an entire secret society."

"An unfair comparison."

We both laughed, quietly. He offered me his hand, and I accepted.

On the way down he stopped to help a young person whose basket had tipped on the slope. We gathered the spilled oranges. The person tried to pay him with one, and he argued cheerfully that the first orange had been payment enough. I bought two so they wouldn't lose the sale.

Back at the Jasmine Dragon, Mina had kept the evening shift running. She passed Iroh a list of repairs rather than asking where he'd been. He thanked her. I put the kettle away.

When the shutters were drawn, he asked whether I would sit with him upstairs for a little while. There was no grand declaration. He was tired. I was tired too.

He kissed me goodnight, gently and with no attempt to make the day's sadness disappear. I stayed until his breathing settled, then turned down the lamp. The hill remained part of his life. I had been allowed to visit it, not claim it.
